summary: This standards-track RFC specifies a VPLS solution that uses VLANs to mark traffic as root or leaf, supporting Ethernet-Tree services. In such a service, roots can talk to everyone, while leaves can talk only to roots and not to each other.

plainLanguage.summary: Picture a teacher who can talk to every student, while students can only talk to the teacher and not to each other.

questions: what are root and leaf in e-tree
how does vpls block leaf to leaf traffic
subtitle: How VPLS can carry Ethernet-Tree services, where leaves reach roots but never each other, using two VLANs.

tldr.problem: An Ethernet-Tree (E-Tree) service must let roots reach everyone while keeping leaves from reaching other leaves. Plain VPLS has no way to tell root traffic from leaf traffic.
tldr.mechanism: Frames are tagged with a root VLAN or a leaf VLAN, carried over ordinary pseudowires, and filtered at egress. LDP and BGP extensions let PEs signal E-Tree support and negotiate VLAN mapping.
tldr.outcome: A single Tree VSI and one set of pseudowires per service can provide E-Tree, using the standard MAC-based forwarding and pseudowire machinery unchanged.

today: RFC 7796 is a Proposed Standard published in March 2016, and the unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It specifies E-Tree support for both LDP VPLS and BGP VPLS.

sections.title: The E-Tree Problem
sections.content:
The Ethernet-Tree (E-Tree) service is defined by the Metro Ethernet Forum in MEF 6.2 as a Rooted-Multipoint Ethernet Virtual Connection service. Frames from a root may be received by any other root or leaf. Frames from a leaf may be received by any root, but must not be received by a leaf. A service may have multiple roots and multiple leaves, and carries both unicast and multicast traffic.

Earlier ideas used the pseudowire control word or the pseudowires themselves to mark root or leaf traffic, but both are applicable only to "VPLS only" networks. RFC 7152 gives the requirements and RFC 7387 an MPLS framework.

This RFC instead reuses the IEEE 802.1Q approach, in which only two VLANs mark traffic: one for frames originating at roots and one for frames originating at leaves. A bridge can then filter leaf-to-leaf frames by VLAN ID. The solution does not change the forwarding table (FIB) and keeps VPLS scalable and simple.
sections.plainLanguage: In this club, the leader can talk to everyone and members can only talk to the leader. Each message carries a colour sticker, and members throw away any message that has the member colour.

sections.title: The PE Model with a Tree VSI
sections.content:
A VPLS PE commonly has a bridge module connected to several Virtual Switching Instances (VSIs). A direct E-Tree design would need two VSIs per PE and two sets of PWs per service, which scales poorly and forces the VSIs to share learned MAC addresses.

The RFC instead specifies a single Tree VSI (T-VSI), a VSI with E-Tree support. The bridge module connects to it with a dual-VLAN virtual interface, so both the root VLAN and the leaf VLAN attach to the same T-VSI. They share one FIB and shared VLAN learning, so only one VPLS instance and one set of PWs is needed per E-Tree service.

Frames from root ACs MUST be tagged with a root VLAN (a root C-VLAN for a C-VLAN bridge, or a root S-VLAN for an 802.1ad bridge). Frames from leaf ACs are tagged with the leaf VLAN in the same way. The outermost VLAN in the Ethernet header is what marks the E-Tree attribute. For S-VLAN tagged ports, a PBB VPLS PE model from RFC 7041 MAY be used instead.
sections.plainLanguage: Rather than building two separate clubhouses, one for leaders and one for members, the club uses one clubhouse and the colour stickers decide who hears what.

sections.title: Pseudowire Encapsulation and VLAN Mapping
sections.content:
T-VSIs MUST be joined by a bidirectional Ethernet PW. It SHOULD use tagged mode (PW type 0x0004 from RFC 4448), and each frame MUST carry a VLAN tag saying whether it came from a root or a leaf. A raw mode PW (type 0x0005) MAY be used for the Compatible mode described below.

VLANs can be handled in two ways. With global VLANs, two VLANs (root and leaf) are used across the whole VPLS network and no mapping is needed. With local VLANs, each PE has its own root and leaf VLANs, which is more scalable in VLAN use but needs a VLAN mapping mechanism in the PW, similar to Section 4.3 of RFC 4448. VLAN parameters can be provisioned or learned through signaling when the PW is set up.
sections.plainLanguage: Everyone can agree on the same two sticker colours, or each site can use its own colours and translate when messages cross between sites.

sections.title: The Three PW Processing Modes
sections.content:
A PE processes frames on each PW in one of three modes.

  • VLAN mapping mode: the PE MUST map the local VLAN to the remote VLAN when sending on the PW, and the remote VLAN to the local VLAN when receiving. The egress bridge then forwards or drops frames by filtering.
  • Compatible mode: used to interwork with a traditional VPLS PE that has only root nodes. The PE MUST remove the root or leaf VLAN when transmitting, and add a tag with the local root VLAN when receiving. A raw PW SHOULD be used.
  • Optimized mode: used when the peer is attached only to leaf nodes. The PE SHOULD drop frames matching its local leaf VLAN ID instead of sending them, which saves bandwidth.

The three flags are kept per PW, and ordinary RFC 4448 PW processing continues in all cases.
sections.plainLanguage: There are three ways to deal with the stickers. Swap them for the other site's colours, take them off for an old-style club that does not use stickers, or skip sending leaf messages to a club that has only members.

sections.title: Signaling with LDP and BGP
sections.content:
For LDP, the RFC defines a new interface parameter sub-TLV, the E-Tree sub-TLV (type 0x1A, length 8). It carries the local root VLAN ID and leaf VLAN ID, a P bit (set when the PE is attached with only leaf nodes) and a V bit (set when the PE can do VLAN mapping). A PE that wants E-Tree MUST include it in its PW Label Mapping message, and the PW type 0x0004 SHOULD be used.

On receipt, the PE first clears the three mode flags. If the VLAN IDs differ and V is clear, a PE that can map VLANs sets VLAN-Mapping-Mode, and otherwise sends a Label Release with the error "E-Tree VLAN mapping not supported". If V is set and both can map, the PE with the minimum IP address sets VLAN-Mapping-Mode. If P is set, a leaf-only PE sends a Label Release with "Leaf-to-Leaf PW released", and any other PE SHOULD set Optimized-Mode. If no E-Tree sub-TLV comes back, the PE SHOULD set up a raw PW and set Compatible-Mode.

For BGP VPLS, an E-Tree extended community (0x800b) carries the same root VLAN, leaf VLAN, P and V values and MUST be attached along with the Layer2 Info Extended Community of RFC 4761. The receive logic mirrors the LDP one. A PE that does not recognize the attribute SHALL ignore it silently.
sections.plainLanguage: When two clubs connect, they swap notes about their sticker colours and whether they can translate. Based on the notes, they decide which of the three ways to talk to each other.

sections.title: OAM and Applicability
sections.content:
The VPLS OAM requirements and framework of RFC 6136 apply, since Ethernet OAM frames and data share the same PW. Service and segment OAM frames SHALL undergo the same VLAN mapping as data, and the root VLAN SHOULD be applied to segment OAM frames so they are not filtered.

The solution applies to both LDP VPLS (RFC 4762) and BGP VPLS (RFC 4761), to VPLS-only networks and to VPLS with Ethernet aggregation, and to PBB VPLS networks. Two appendices show other PE models: one with a VSI and no bridge, and one with an external E-Tree interface.
sections.plainLanguage: Health-check messages get the same sticker translation as normal ones, and they use the leader sticker so nobody throws them away.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The solution requires implementations to block leaf-to-leaf communication in the VPLS data plane. If all PEs enforce this, attacks from one leaf to another are avoided. However, if a PE is compromised or misconfigured, a leaf may be treated as a root and receive traffic from other leaves inappropriately.

Authenticity and integrity measures for LDP need to be considered as in RFC 5036, and the security considerations of RFC 4448, RFC 4761 and RFC 4762 also apply.
sections.plainLanguage: The rule only works if every club follows it. If one club cheats, members may start hearing each other.

sections.title: IANA Assignments
sections.content: IANA allocated sub-TLV value 0x1A (length 8) for E-Tree in the Pseudowire Interface Parameters Sub-TLV type registry. It also allocated two LDP status codes: 0x20000003 "E-Tree VLAN mapping not supported" and 0x20000004 "Leaf-to-Leaf PW released". For BGP, the E-Tree Info sub-type 0x0b (type 0x80) was allocated in the Generic Transitive Experimental Use Extended Community Sub-Types registry.
sections.plainLanguage: The official number keepers wrote down the new labels so nobody else would use the same ones.

items.label: Map local and remote VLANs
items.desc: Local VLAN to remote VLAN on transmit, remote to local on receive.

items.label: Peer is a traditional root-only VSI
items.desc: Remove the VLAN on transmit, add the local root VLAN on receive.

items.label: Peer has only leaf nodes
items.desc: Drop frames with the local leaf VLAN instead of sending them.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: Length of the sub-TLV in octets.

fields.name: Reserved
fields.desc: Set to zero on transmit, ignored on receive.

fields.name: P
fields.desc: Leaf-only bit: 1 if the PE is attached with only leaf nodes.

fields.name: V
fields.desc: Set if the sender is capable of VLAN mapping.

fields.name: Root VLAN ID
fields.desc: Value of the local root VLAN.

fields.name: Leaf VLAN ID
fields.desc: Value of the local leaf VLAN.
